voyage.name: Edinburgh International Festival
voyage.content: The original that spawned all the rest. Founded in 1947 and still seen as more "high-brow" than any of its offspring. Surprisingly, tickets are often priced more reasonably than for many Fringe shows. Some events have preview performances at a much lower price.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Military Tattoo
voyage.content: One of the iconic images of Edinburgh for millions worldwide is the yearly Tattoo, kilted pipers skirling below the battlements of Edinburgh Castle. Although tickets sell out well in advance, persevering individuals are likely to find one or two tickets still for sale due to cancellations. Just be prepared to ask, ask, and ask again! There are usually fireworks at the end of the shows which can also be seen from e.g.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Festival Fringe
voyage.content: As the name might suggest, this festival developed on the fringe of the main International Festival and offers more alternative performances, with an emphasis on comedy and avant-garde; it is now the largest arts festival in the world. Many shows offer cheaper preview tickets on the first two days of the festival or a 2-for-1 ticket special on two selected dates. There are a few sub-festivals that are part of the Fri

voyage.name: Edinburgh Jazz and Blues Festival
voyage.content: Festival of about 150 concerts in 11 venues.

voyage.name: Edinburgh International Book Festival
voyage.content: Takes place in a temporary village of marquees at Charlotte Square Gardens (West End of George Street, New Town).

voyage.name: Edinburgh Art Festival
voyage.content: Some permanent outdoor commissions which can be seen all year, and temporary exhibitions and events during the festival.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Mela
voyage.content: Multicultural festival held in Leith.

voyage.name: Edinburgh International Television Festival
voyage.content: Predominantly a "closed shop" for industry professionals only.

voyage.name: Edinburgh International Science Festival
voyage.content: Takes place annually in March or April. Emphasis on "hands-on" science.

voyage.name: Beltane Fire Festival
voyage.content: Fire Festival marking the beginning of summer (evening of April 30). The festival has its origins in the pre-Christian Celtic festival of the same name, which was held to herald the coming of spring and to celebrate the fertility of the countryside. Drums, dancing, semi-nudity, pagan ritual, home-brew and lots of fire and fireworks. Crowds of around 12,000 enjoy the ceremony and spectacle every year. For the full tra

voyage.name: Hidden Door
voyage.content: Annual non-profit art, music, theatre, etc. event taking place in unused spaces in the city that change from year to year. End of May/beginning of June.

voyage.name: Degree Show
voyage.address: Edinburgh College of Art, Old Town
voyage.content: Around the end of May the Edinburgh College of Art opens its doors and exhibits the works on art, design and architecture of their students. A similar event, the Masters Degree Show, takes place in August as part of the Edinburgh Art Festival. See the ECA event calendar for details.

voyage.name: Imaginate Festival
voyage.content: Every May/June, an international festival of children's theatre.

voyage.name: Meadows Festival
voyage.content: A free festival in the Meadows (South) on a weekend in early June with lots of food stalls, second-hand merchandise and live music.

voyage.name: Edinburgh International Film Festival
voyage.content: Now moved to June from its former slot in August, so that it no longer clashes with all the others! Centred around the Filmhouse Cinema on Lothian Road, though other cinemas take part too. In 2022 it is back in August, but it is not clear if this is a permanent change.

voyage.name: Samhuinn Fire Festival
voyage.content: Fire Festival marking the beginning of winter (evening of October 31). Procession and enacted fight between the King of Summer and Prince of Winter with great accompanying percussion.

voyage.name: Guy Fawkes Night
voyage.content: Evening of November 5. With ticketed fireworks (£6.50) in the Meadowbank Sports Centre (East). Can be seen (for free) from several locations in the city.

voyage.name: St Andrew's Day
voyage.content: Celebrate St Andrew's Day, Scotland's national day on November 30. There are many free events on the nearest weekend in Edinburgh. Historic Scotland opens many of its sites for free (free tickets are required and can be booked online).

voyage.name: Edinburgh Castle
voyage.price: Adult £19.50, child (7-15) £11.40, conc £15.50, Historic Scotland / English Heritage / Cadw free
voyage.content: Iconic fortress perched magnificently on a volcanic rock above the city. The castle has been continuously used for 1100 years and is kept in excellent condition; it's still the ceremonial headquarters of the army in Scotland. Highlights include the Great Hall, the Honours of Scotland (the Scottish Crown Jewels), the War Museum and the 12th century St Margaret's Chapel. The One O'Clock Gun is fired each day from Mills

voyage.name: Camera Obscura
voyage.content: Over 150 years old, the Camera Obscura projects light from the top of the tower onto a large dish in a dark room below, displaying a panorama of the city. The effect still works on overcast days or at night but is best in sunlight, when you can use a sheet of paper to "pick up" people seen in the streets and have them scurry in your hand. The tower also houses a gallery of optical illusions that wouldn't be out of pl

voyage.name: Gladstone's Land
voyage.price: Adult £10, conc £8.50, child £6, NTS / NT free
voyage.content: Thomas Gladstone was a wealthy merchant, and in 1617 he had this house refashioned to accommodate his family and to partly rent out. A "Land" means a tall narrow townhouse from the period when Old Town was cramped and the only space for development was upwards. Typically along the Royal Mile the ground floor was shops and trade, genteel folk lived on the first and second floors, and lower-income residents had to lump

voyage.name: Writers' Museum
voyage.content: This museum, in a tall house built in 1622, celebrates three Scottish literary giants: Robert Burns, Sir Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson. From 1719 the close was the residence of the widow of the 1st Earl of Stair, who ordered the Glencoe massacre.

voyage.name: St Giles
voyage.content: It's often called a Cathedral, but the Church of Scotland brooks no such episcopal entity, and Charles I dubbing it "cathedral" in 1633 was one reason his head was chopped off. Safer to call it "High Kirk", though they're nowadays lenient with first time offenders. The present building is from 14th century with much Victorian Gothic, notably its crowned spire. Highlight is the Chapel of the Order of the Thistle, Scot

voyage.name: Mary King's Close
voyage.content: Mary King (1590-1644) was a clothes merchant and city burgess. She died the year before plague struck and carried off the rest of her family. In 1753 Royal Exchange, now City Chambers, was built over several closes by demolishing their upper storeys, while the lower storeys were used for storage then later blocked off. This means a warren of medieval alleys and low dwellings has been preserved, re-opened in 2003 and

voyage.name: Museum of Childhood
voyage.content: Concepts and imagery of childhood are ever-changing. See if you can find your (or your grandparents') old toys in the collection, and your place in history.

voyage.name: The Peoples' Story Museum
voyage.content: This is housed in Canongate Tolbooth, the medieval centre for governance and justice (preferably gruesome) as Canongate was a separate jurisdiction until 1856. The museum covers the story of working class life, and of organised labour, from the late 18th century to the present.

voyage.name: Canongate Kirk
voyage.hours: Open Sun afternoon, otherwise erratic; Services Sun 10:30
voyage.content: In 1687 James VII (II of England) chucked the Protestants out of Holyrood to convert it to a royal Roman Catholic chapel, the sort of behaviour that got him ousted from the monarchy the following year. The congregation moved to Infirmary St then to this building on its completion in 1691. From 1952 Queen Elizabeth II regularly attended when at Holyrood, and in 2011 her granddaughter Zara Phillips married former Engla

voyage.name: Museum of Edinburgh
voyage.content: Museum of city history in a mustard-hued mansion built in 1570.

voyage.name: Dunbar's Close Garden
voyage.content: This close was re-modelled in the 1970s to recreate a 17th-century physic and knot garden, a hidden quiet place in the busy city.

voyage.name: Scottish Parliament
voyage.hours: Mon Fri Sat and public holidays 10AM-5PM, Tue-Thu 9AM-6:30PM
voyage.content: A unique building, designed by Spanish Catalan architect Enric Miralles, completed in 2004. It's either a daring showpiece of postmodern architecture or a national embarrassment or a bit of both, time will tell. Parliament meets Tu-Th and you can watch debates from the Public Gallery, ask for tickets at reception. First Minister's Question Time is normally Th noon-12:45PM, and you need to reserve this up to 7 days in

voyage.name: Dynamic Earth
voyage.content: Interactive natural history museum exhibiting the forces and features of our planet: volcanoes, polar ice, rainforests and so on. Opened in 1999, it's a tent-like structure on the former site of a gasworks and brewery.

voyage.name: Holyrood Palace
voyage.hours: Nov-Mar Thu-Mon 9:30AM - 4:30PM, Apr-Oct Thu-Mon (& daily Jul-Sep) 9:30AM - 6PM
voyage.content: The Palace is a royal residence, closed when the king is here for a week in July and for similar state occasions. It's been repeatedly smashed up and rebuilt, and the present building is mostly from the 1670s. Highlights are the grand stair, state apartments, throne room, Mary Queen of Scots Chambers (where bloodstains from the murder of Rizzio are still visible), King's Gallery a sample of the royal art collection,

voyage.name: George IV Bridge
voyage.content: This high-level road courses south from the top of High Street and spans the hollow of Grassmarket. Completed in 1836, it's lined with Victorian and modern buildings such as the two libraries. Victoria Street descends into the hollow, while Victoria Terrace is a walkway above it that loops back onto Royal Mile.

voyage.name: National Library of Scotland
voyage.content: A venerable reference library, which you need membership to access, but it has public exhibitions about literature. "Treasures" is its permanent exhibition. But don't stumble in here mistaking it for Central Library across the street.

voyage.name: Central Library
voyage.content: See Edinburgh#Connect for how to access. The internet stations are in the Learning Centre, and the building houses Central Lending Library, Central Reference Library, Central Children's Library, Edinburgh and Scottish Collections, Art & Design Library and Music Library. It has a wealth of material for research such as old newspapers and maps, but births, marriages and deaths are filed at East Register House by the bu

voyage.name: Greyfriars Kirk
voyage.content: This church was built in 1620 on the grounds of an abandoned Franciscan Friary, but seriously damaged by later calamities or Acts of God so the present structure is mostly Victorian. It remains active, as other Presbyterian churches have closed and their congregations moved here. The main visitor interest is the ancient graveyard: notable denizens include the architects William and John Adam, the notorious hell-rake

voyage.name: National Museum of Scotland
voyage.content: Superb museum of Scotland's heritage. You enter into the lofty Victorian Grand Gallery, where the millennium clock chimes on the hour. Exhibition halls cover Scottish and world history and culture, science, technology, art and design, and natural history. Dolly the sheep, the 12th-century Lewis chess pieces, and dinosaurs are some of the highlights. NMS also run the War Museum in the castle, the Museum of Flight near

voyage.name: Anatomical Museum
voyage.hours: Last Sat of Sept-Nov and Jan-May
voyage.address: Doorway 3, Medical School, Teviot Place EH8 9AG
voyage.content: Large collection of anatomical specimens and life and death masks. Best known is the skeleton of William Burke, hanged in 1829 after he and William Hare killed at least 16 people to sell the bodies for dissection. Limited opening as the area is in continual use for teaching, booking essential.

voyage.name: St Cecilia's Hall
voyage.content: Scotland's oldest purpose-built concert hall, opened in 1763 and still in regular use. It hosts the University of Edinburgh collection of historic musical instruments, crafted 16th to 20th century, many of which (such as the Trompette Demilune) are no longer played.

voyage.name: Talbot Rice Gallery
voyage.content: David Talbot Rice (1903-72) was in the louche crowd at Oxford that inspired Brideshead Revisited and became a distinguished scholar of East Mediterranean and Russian art, with extensive contacts in those parts - how come this fellow was never implicated in a spy ring? His spell as University Vice Principal is commemorated in this gallery with changing exhibitions of contemporary art. It's housed within Old College of

voyage.name: Dovecot Studios
voyage.content: Tapestry studio and gallery housed in the former public baths. There is a cafe, shop, and viewing gallery where you can look down on weavers at work.

voyage.name: Surgeons' Hall Museums
voyage.content: The permanent exhibitions are the Pathology Museum, the History of Surgery and the Dental Museum. Not suitable for children under 10 as the exhibits include human remains.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Central Mosque
voyage.content: Stately mosque and minaret completed in 1998 in a modern variant of Turkish style. You can generally look in between prayer times.

voyage.name: City Art Centre
voyage.content: Four-floor gallery run by the city council. They rotate artwork from their extensive Scottish collection and have changing exhibitions.

voyage.name: Fruitmarket
voyage.content: Gallery of contemporary art, refurbished in 2018. From 1936 to the 1970s this was where soft fruit and veg were traded, handy for the trains and delivery vans.

voyage.name: Stills
voyage.content: Photography gallery with three exhibitions a year. They also support photographers through courses and hire of equipment, darkroom and digital lab.

voyage.name: Museum on the Mound
voyage.content: Museum about money and coins, in the basement of the Palladian pile of the former Bank of Scotland headquarters. Scotland developed a banking sector in the 18th century to support long-distance trade, and still prints its own banknotes.

voyage.name: The Edinburgh Dungeon
voyage.content: "Haunted House" experience, where you take a 70 min tour through 11 shows and 2 rides loosely based on Scotland's horrible history: William Wallace, Mary King's Ghost, cannibal Sawney Bean, Burke and Hare and more.

voyage.name: Escape The Past
voyage.content: Immersive escape rooms and outdoor puzzle trails based on Edinburgh's history. Experiences include historically accurate props, live actors and special effects. Housed in the basement of a 19th Century Methodist Church. Highlights include "The Anatomist" a 60 minute escape room based on Edinburgh's grave-robbing-era medical history.

voyage.name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
voyage.content: Tour of the history and craft of whisky distilling, with expert guides - the basic or "silver" tour works well for beginners. They have a huge selection; the core of it is the 3384 bottles collected by Brazilian whisky enthusiast Claive Vidiz.

voyage.name: The Lost Close
voyage.content: Underground experiences and tours led by expert Storytellers. Whisky, gin and beer tastings available - starting from £15.

voyage.name: Monkey Barrel Comedy
voyage.content: Intimate comedy venue with several acts each night. Drink and some food available.

voyage.name: Festival Theatre
voyage.content: Large performance venue, home of the Scottish Ballet and Scottish Opera. It also hosts contemporary dance, ballet, musicals and panto.

voyage.name: Reid Concert Hall
voyage.content: General Reid (1721-1807) endowed the School of Music at the University of Edinburgh. They put on occasional free lunchtime concerts here, especially on 13 Feb, Reid's birthday. You may also be able to look in on their collection of antique instruments.

voyage.name: Usher Hall
voyage.content: The city's main concert hall, capacity 2200, and home to the Royal Scottish National Orchestra. It was completed in 1914, funded by Andrew Usher the whisky distiller and blender.

voyage.name: Royal Lyceum
voyage.content: Completed in 1883 and little altered since, this is home to the Royal Lyceum Theatre Company.

voyage.name: Traverse Theatre
voyage.content: Since 1992 this has hosted Traverse theatre company, dedicated to new works.

voyage.name: King's Theatre
voyage.content: Reopened in August 2026 after 4 years of refurbishment.

voyage.name: Cameo Cinema
voyage.content: Mainstream, arthouse and alternative films, with an Edwardian interior.

voyage.name: Odeon Cinema
voyage.content: Mostly mainstream movies.

voyage.name: Red Door Gallery
voyage.content: Arts and crafts and giftware.

voyage.name: Armstrongs
voyage.content: A local institution, this has a huge stock of vintage clothing and uniforms, including pre-hirpled kilts.

voyage.name: Underground Solu'shn
voyage.content: A great little record store dealing mainly in dance/electro music.

voyage.name: Cadenhead's Whisky Shop
voyage.content: This Campbeltown-based firm is an independent bottler of whisky and other spirits (a rarity nowadays), so they do bespoke sales and samplers.

voyage.name: Focus
voyage.content: Skatewear and skateboard store, friendly knowledgeable staff.

voyage.name: The Piemaker
voyage.content: This has a wide range of delicious pies and savoury pastries, piping hot. They're mostly a takeaway and don't deliver, but have a few seats inside.

voyage.name: Kebab Mahal
voyage.content: Good halal curries, kebabs and tandooris, no alcohol.

voyage.name: The Original Mosque Kitchen
voyage.content: Inexpensive chicken or vegetable curry. A favorite with generations of Edinburgh University students for its cost and portion sizes.

voyage.name: Tempting Tattie
voyage.content: Inexpensive takeaway for trad baked potatoes.

voyage.name: Kampong Ah Lee
voyage.content: Tasty Malaysian dishes such as Roti Canai, Satay, Nasi Lemak, Laksa and Rendang.

voyage.name: Em’s Kitchen
voyage.content: Full Scottish breakfast, shakshuka, coffee and tea options, with seating that looks into a quiet car park and garden.

voyage.name: John's Coffee House & Tavern
voyage.content: Located in a historic building. Breakfast, all-day waffles, light lunch options, small plates to share, bar with wide range of Scotch whiskies.

voyage.name: The Everest
voyage.content: Good inexpensive Nepalese and Indian food.

voyage.name: Petit Paris
voyage.content: Traditional French restaurant complete with chequered tablecloths and whitewashed walls.

voyage.name: David Bann
voyage.content: Imaginative and tasty vegetarian food, with lots available for vegans or GF.

voyage.name: Whiski
voyage.content: A bit touristy, but a good choice for Scottish food, drink and music. Hundreds of whiskies available, bar staff happy to advise. Live music every night from 9:30PM, try to sit up front for this.

voyage.name: Nok's Kitchen
voyage.content: Decent Thai food with vegetarian options. They add 10% service to the menu prices.

voyage.name: Kanpai Sushi
voyage.content: Small portions of sushi and other Japanese food, and pricey, but speedy service and memorable quality.

voyage.name: Gurkha
voyage.content: Traditional Indian and Nepalese restaurant.

voyage.name: Kalpana
voyage.content: Long-established quality vegetarian Indian restaurant serving curries, thalis and tandooris.

voyage.name: Tanjore
voyage.content: One of the few places in Edinburgh serving South Indian food such as Dosas, Uttapams, Sambar and other Tamil specialities.

voyage.name: MUMS
voyage.content: Classic British comfort food: haggis, fish & chips, sausage & mash, stews, or shepherd's pie. Lots of veggie choices, no reservations.

voyage.name: The Elephant House
voyage.content: Consistently good coffee and light bites, cafe is full of university and creative types; JK Rowling wrote much of the first Harry Potter book here. And that alas is the problem: it's become part of the Potter circus, every half hour sees another coachload of tourists all craning for selfies and trying to nick the cutlery and scrawling graffiti in the loo. Prices, service and ambience have suffered accordingly, and Ro

voyage.name: The Witchery by the Castle
voyage.content: By the castle entrance, The Witchery serves top-class food in an elegant candle-lit restaurant. They've now added rooms, flamboyantly camp.

voyage.name: Timberyard
voyage.content: Outstanding Scottish cuisine in a 19th century warehouse, with extensive wine list. One Michelin star, the head chef is Jimmy Murray.

voyage.name: The Jolly Judge
voyage.hours: Tue Wed noon-11PM, Thu-Sat, Mon noon-midnight, Sun 2PM-11PM
voyage.content: Cosy independent pub with a good selection of beer and whisky. One of the few pubs on Royal Mile that's not a tourist trap.

voyage.name: Albanach
voyage.content: Cosy Belhaven pub with food and whisky.

voyage.name: Doctors
voyage.content: Now a Belhaven pub, this is a welcoming place with good ales and food. It was a few yards from the former Royal Infirmary, within bleep range and sprinting distance for the junior doctors.

voyage.name: Sandy Bells
voyage.content: Likewise frequented by medical students, this has live folk music every night.

voyage.name: The Pear Tree
voyage.content: Popular with students, this has a large beer garden and outdoor big screen for TV sports.

voyage.name: The Kilderkin
voyage.content: Fair selection of cask ales and whisky, the food is so-so and the warmth of welcome varies. This is the original of a chain that now includes The Windsor on Elm Row, Blue Blazer on Spittal St and Bennets at Tolcross.

voyage.name: The Bow Bar
voyage.content: Old-style boozer with a large selection of whiskies, selection of guest ales, and no background music.

voyage.name: Bennets Bar
voyage.content: A good old-fashioned pub, now part of Kilderkin group, with a wide selection of real ale and whisky. It is traditionally the place for pre / post-theatre drinks, with the Kings Theatre.

voyage.name: The Bongo Club
voyage.content: A café-bar and live music venue.

voyage.name: Cabaret Voltaire
voyage.content: Atmospheric basement vault with regular gigs.

voyage.name: Dragonfly
voyage.content: Well-hidden but popular cocktail lounge.

voyage.name: The Jazz Bar
voyage.content: Live music every night, majoring on jazz; early shows are generally free, later gigs individually priced. Limited food or seating.

voyage.name: The Liquid Room
voyage.content: 800-capacity live music venue.

voyage.name: Wash Bar
voyage.content: Modern pub, mostly a local crowd, TV sport, no food.

voyage.name: 56 North
voyage.content: Cocktail bar incorporating South Loch gin distillery.

voyage.name: Motel One Edinburgh Royal
voyage.content: Comfy efficient place by the station, great value. They have another branch by the bus station.

voyage.name: Kick Ass Greyfriars
voyage.content: Cheerful friendly staff and modern amenities. Offers dormitory beds and 2-4 bed private rooms.

voyage.name: Code The Court
voyage.content: Hybrid hostel/hotel in a former jail and courtroom. Offers pod capsules and private rooms.

voyage.name: Castle Rock Hostel
voyage.content: Clean spacious hostel with 300 beds on the hill just below Castle Esplanade.

voyage.name: ibis Edinburgh Centre South Bridge
voyage.content: Reliable chain hotel.

voyage.name: ibis Edinburgh Centre Royal Mile - Hunter Square
voyage.content: Slick welcoming inexpensive hotel.

voyage.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh City Centre
voyage.content: Good reliable chain hotel by the station.

voyage.name: Leonardo Royal Hotel
voyage.content: Good value place next to the railway station.

voyage.name: Ten Hill Place Hotel
voyage.content: Central but quiet hotel in a Georgian terrace with 78 bedrooms.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn Express
voyage.content: They call it "Royal Mile" but it's in the dark canyon of Cowgate 200 yards south - still a very central location, and value for money.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Holyrood Hotel
voyage.content: Now part of Marriott chain, this is under renovation but remains open.

voyage.name: Apex Grassmarket
voyage.content: Comfy place to stay with great views of the castle.

voyage.name: Apex City of Edinburgh
voyage.content: Similar price and quality to their branch at No 31.

voyage.name: Hotel du Vin
voyage.content: Great comfort, service and location beyond its price bracket.

voyage.name: Novotel
voyage.content: Mid-range chain near Tolcross.

voyage.name: DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel Edinburgh City Centre
voyage.content: Comfy hotel near Usher Hall, short walk to the castle.

voyage.name: The Scotsman
voyage.content: This iconic building stands like a castle guarding the entrance to Old Town from North Bridge. From 1904 to 2001 it housed The Scotsman newspaper, with editors and reporters above, printing presses below, and newspapers loaded onto trains from the basement. After they moved out it became an upscale hotel, charmingly refurbished within and scoring highly for comfort, service and location.

voyage.name: Hilton Edinburgh Carlton
voyage.content: Great location, service and comfort mostly good, some construction noise.

voyage.name: Sheraton Grand Hotel
voyage.content: Part of Marriott chain, great location and for most visitors great comfort, but housekeeping is too erratic for what you pay.

voyage.name: Radisson Blu Hotel
voyage.content: Great location, comfort and service. The hotel was built in 1990, but with a retro-antique facade to blend with neighbouring buildings.

voyage.name: Cheval Old Town Chambers
voyage.content: This knock-through of medieval tenements was designed as luxury serviced apartments, but has added common areas to create a townhouse hotel.

voyage.name: Radisson Collection Hotel
voyage.content: Closed for refurbishment.

voyage.name: Calton Hill
voyage.content: This is the stubby crag just east of Princes Street: a short stroll up it commands great views. The "National Monument", a memorial to Scots killed in the Napoleonic Wars, was an attempt to out-do the Parthenon in Athens but the money ran out with only the west facade built. Nelson's Tower was built 1807-16 in the shape of an upturned telescope in honour of the naval hero. A Time Ball on the mast drops at 1PM every d

voyage.name: Old Calton Cemetery
voyage.content: Atmospheric Georgian graves, memorials, and funerary ornaments. Memorials include those to the philosopher David Hume (1711-1776), to the Scots who died in the American Civil War, and to the Martyrs of Reform imprisoned or transported for sedition in the 1790s for calling for the right to vote.

voyage.name: St Andrew's & St George's West Church
voyage.content: Completed in 1784, this is the parish church of the New Town. It's Italianate with an unusual elliptical interior, with an ornate ceiling blending Roman, Pompeian and Scottish elements. The steeple holds Scotland's oldest complete peal of bells, cast in 1788. In 1843 this church was the scene of The Great Disruption, when a third of ministers broke with the Presbyterian Church of Scotland to found their own Free Kirk

voyage.name: Scott Monument
voyage.content: Sir Walter Scott (1771-1832) re-invented Scotland. In the late Georgian era, he popularised tales of its medieval and Jacobean tumults, and created the clan tartans you buy on Princes St. This grand Gothic memorial, part cathedral part moon rocket, was completed in 1846 to dominate the east end of Princes St. It's 200 ft 6 in / 61.1 m tall, and guided tours take you up 287 steps (no lift) to the top platform, for a c

voyage.name: Royal Scottish Academy
voyage.content: An august neo-classical building on The Mound, fronting onto Princes St, and its main function is to be confused with the National Gallery behind. The RSA is a separate organisation promoting contemporary Scottish art. The building hosts temporary exhibitions but doesn't have a permanent display - the Academy's extensive collection is dispersed across many galleries. That might include your own home, as they run an a

voyage.name: National Galleries of Scotland: National
voyage.price: Free, charges for major temporary exhibitions
voyage.content: This holds much of Scotland's fine artwork from Renaissance to 20th century, with changing exhibitions. These rotate seasonally, so an exhibition put on for the Festival typically stays to the end of the year, allowing quieter times to view. Enter from the plaza between gallery and Royal Scottish Academy, and a basement passage connects the two exhibition spaces. The Scottish Galleries on the lowest floor reopened in

voyage.name: National Galleries of Scotland: Portrait
voyage.content: Completed in 1890, this is a striking red sandstone neo-Gothic building. It holds portraits of Scots from down the ages, with new faces being added all the time: Billy Connolly and Tilda Swinton mingle with Mary Queen of Scots. The entrance hall has a grand frieze of notable Scots in procession.

voyage.name: Palestine Museum
voyage.content: A branch of their main museum in Woodbridge Connecticut, this is mostly artwork with exhibitions on the Nakhba and other events.

voyage.name: Princes Street Gardens
voyage.content: The west portion fills the valley beyond the Mound, spanning the railway tracks to the foot of castle crag. The east portion is the terrace around the Scott Monument. They were laid out in the 1820s as private gardens for residents of the street: occupants of bath chairs required a medical certificate that their condition was not contagious. Their initial opening to the public was solely at Christmas and New Year, in

voyage.name: The Georgian House
voyage.content: This townhouse was designed by Robert Adam, completed in 1796 and has been furnished in the style of its first owner John Lamont. Its last private owner the Marquess of Bute also acquired adjacent townhouses and along with the other owners got the entire north facade of the square restored to Adams' imposing original design. Visit by self-guided tour, and in mid-summer you need to book as it sells out.

voyage.name: Charlotte Square
voyage.content: In front of the house is the mirror-image of St Andrew's Square at the east end of George St. Bute House at Number 6, next door to The Georgian House, is the official residence of the First Minister of Scotland, so you might see a motorcade, TV cameras and armed security outside. The gardens in the square are private. Prince Albert stands in the middle, with his view down the street somewhat impeded by mature trees.

voyage.name: Gilbert the Phone Box
voyage.content: An old red phone box has been kitted out with Edwardian memorabilia, and nicknamed for Sir Giles Gilbert Scott (1880-1960) designer of the box. You can look in the windows anytime, or collect the key for £3 (for Save the Children) from Stewart Christie and Co who run a long established gentleman's outfitter in the shop next to it.

voyage.name: James Clerk Maxwell's Birthplace
voyage.content: Isaac Newton realised that what caused the apple to fall was the very same force moving the moon, planets and stars. James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879) was born in this house, before the family moved to Kirkcudbright. He was intensely curious about how nature worked and made a "great unification" of equal importance to Newton's: that magnetism, electricity, light and heat are all manifestations of the same electromagnet

voyage.name: Dean Village
voyage.content: It is an attractive hamlet down in the dene - the steep valley - of the Water of Leith. It was the medieval crossing point on the route from Edinburgh to South Queensferry, and is the main access point for this section of the Water of Leith Walkway (described below). The fast-descending stream drove 11 grain mills here, so it was the powerbase for the Baxters, the bakers' merchant guild. The present bridge across the

voyage.name: Dean Bridge
voyage.content: is best seen from below in Dean Village as you follow the walkway along the stream - from the top it's just a busy thoroughfare. Crossing in four arches 107 ft / 32 m above the stream, it was Telford's last major project. As well as improving the route to Fife, it made the north bank into prime real estate, so elegant terraces were built there.

voyage.name: National Galleries of Scotland: Modern One
voyage.content: The original modern art gallery, established in 1960, was in the Botanic Gardens. In 1895 it moved into this neoclassical building, originally a refuge for fatherless children, and in 1999 it expanded across the road into the neoclassical orphanage now known as Modern Two. The gardens of Modern One have been sculpted. Both buildings have extensive contemporary collections and most visitors find that seeing one of the

voyage.name: Modern Two
voyage.content: Opposite side of Belford Rd has a slightly smaller collection, but enough to infuriate about one-in-five reviewers, who rage that their kids' drawings stuck on the fridge door are better. A neon sign in the garden reassures all and sundry that "There will be no miracles".

voyage.name: St Mary's Episcopal Cathedral
voyage.content: This stonking great neo-Gothic church was completed in 1879, designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott, with the towers added in 1917. It's the senior Episcopal church in Scotland, within the Anglican tradition of bishops (and much else) that the Presbyterians rejected. It has daily choral services: the song school (open occasionally) has stunning murals by Phoebe Anna Traquair.

voyage.name: St Mary's Metropolitan Cathedral
voyage.content: The Roman Catholic Cathedral was established as a chapel in 1814 and became a cathedral in 1886 for the archdiocese of Edinburgh and St Andrews. It was designed by James Gillespie Graham in neo-perpendicular style and has undergone several alterations and extensions - in the 1970s the tenements that hemmed it in were demolished. There are services twice daily in English and daily in Polish.

voyage.name: Sherlock Holmes
voyage.content: His creator Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (1859-1930) was born nearby at 11 Picardy Place, to a genteel but impoverished Irish Catholic family. His first Sherlock story was published in 1886. The statue was in storage while the plaza was remodelled around the tramlines but restored in June 2023.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Playhouse
voyage.content: Built as a cinema in 1929 and refurbished in 1980, this is now Scotland's largest performance space, with a capacity of 3059. That's about 1000 more than can comfortably be seated and 2000 more than they have toilet provision for. It's run by ATG, Ambassador Theatre Group.

voyage.name: Vue
voyage.content: Large multiplex cinema showing mainstream releases.

voyage.name: St James Quarter
voyage.content: Shopping centre which opened in 2021, replacing the tired St James Centre, includes John Lewis department store, and 3 floors of mid- and up-market chain stores. Also here are the W Hotel, Roomzzz aparthotel and several restaurants. Too bad about the curling tapered roof sculpture, which looks like a . . . well, enough to spoil the view.

voyage.name: Waverley Market
voyage.content: Upmarket mainstream shops in a covered mall above Waverley station.

voyage.name: Slater Menswear
voyage.content: Eastern outpost of the famous Glasgow institution. Broad range at keen prices with helpful service.

voyage.name: Paper Tiger
voyage.content: Classy selection of cards, home accessories, toys and gifts. Their other branches are at 53 Lothian Rd and 194 Morningside Rd.

voyage.name: The Dragonfly
voyage.content: Funky little shop with a lovely range of cards and gifts.

voyage.name: Crombies
voyage.content: Award-winning butchers shop, established 1955. Great quality local meat, especially their range of sausages.

voyage.name: Real Foods
voyage.content: The original Edinburgh "health food" shop, opened in 1975. Sells a wide range of loose and packet dried goods, some vegetarian ready meals and snacks and a small selection of organic fruit and veg.

voyage.name: Valvona & Crolla
voyage.content: Legendary Italian deli founded in 1934. Its grey frontage is unassuming, but it stretches back through a wonderland of food. There's a small bright cafe in the back, where you'll be lucky to get seated.

voyage.name: Vinyl Villains
voyage.content: Second-hand vinyl record shop with a great selection, quality stock and reasonable prices. They also have CDs, T-shirts, posters and fanzines.

voyage.name: Harburn Hobbies
voyage.content: Family-run business established in the 1930s. Specialises in model railways, including some items exclusive to this shop. Also die-cast model vehicles, Scalextric slot car racing systems and plastic and wooden model construction kits.

voyage.name: Snax
voyage.content: A small fast-food joint, limited seating. The food is cheap and edible, with a decent vegetarian selection.

voyage.name: Cafe Piccante
voyage.content: Unashamed specialists in late-night greasy food, friendly staff and a DJ at weekends. The burgers are a stand-out and deep-fried Mars bars are available for tourists.

voyage.name: Cafe Royal
voyage.content: Beautifully tiled Victorian palace of a pub, designed in 1862 as a showroom for the latest fixtures and fittings, no dogs. The stylish restaurant serves seafood and other classics.

voyage.name: Dishoom
voyage.content: Scottish outpost of a small national chain, modelling their interiors on colonial Bombay cafes. The food is made to share, mostly consisting of small plates, with the house chaat, black daal and salli botti particularly memorable. Often busy, but they can usually squeeze you in, remember those Bombay buses and commuter trains.

voyage.name: The Dome
voyage.content: Bar and grill in a former bank headquarters with grand exterior and impressive interior.

voyage.name: Pizza Pilgrims
voyage.content: This Neapolitan-style chain pizzeria opened its Edinburgh outlet in 2025 to much hype. It's good not great.

voyage.name: Mussel Inn
voyage.content: Seafood restaurant owned by shellfish producers, ingredients direct from the west coast.

voyage.name: Dulse
voyage.content: This serves excellent Scottish seafood.

voyage.name: Teuchters
voyage.content: Lively pub serving modern Scottish cuisine at reasonable prices.

voyage.name: Café Marlayne
voyage.content: Chic cosy French bistro serving up excellent French cuisine.

voyage.name: Cafe St Honoré
voyage.address: Thistle Street North West Lane EH2 1EA
voyage.content: Great continental food and wine. Gluten free and dairy free menus available.

voyage.name: Contini
voyage.content: Restaurant in a former grand banking hall serving wonderful Italian food.

voyage.name: Holy Cow
voyage.content: Excellent basement vegan cafe. Home-made food.

voyage.name: The Palmerston
voyage.content: Chicly decorated restaurant and bakery in a former bank, the menu changes daily.

voyage.name: Voodoo Rooms
voyage.content: Over-the-top decor in this quirky pub, sometimes has live entertainment, mixed reviews for the food.

voyage.name: All Bar One
voyage.content: Chain pub with slick service and good ale and meals.

voyage.name: Eastside
voyage.content: Busy cocktail bar and night entertainment spot.

voyage.name: The Standing Order
voyage.content: A cavernous converted bank building. It's part of the JD Wetherspoon chain and always has a wide range of inexpensive drinks and pub food.

voyage.name: Tonic
voyage.content: A great cocktail bar with friendly helpful staff.

voyage.name: The Oxford Bar
voyage.content: Trad drouthy Scottish pub, often a setting in the Ian Rankin "Inspector Rebus" novels.

voyage.name: The Kenilworth
voyage.content: Splendidly tiled and wood-panelled pub.

voyage.name: Mathers
voyage.content: Traditional bar with a good range of real ales and whisky, reasonable pub food. Big screen for football and rugby.

voyage.name: The Basement
voyage.content: Nowadays specialising in Mexico, so this is the place for tequila or tacos.

voyage.name: Barony Bar
voyage.content: Trad pub, dog-friendly, sometimes has live music. It calls itself a gastropub but customers don't much rate the food.

voyage.name: The Cask & Barrel
voyage.content: This often features in the novels of Christopher Brookmyre as the pub where journalist "Jack Parlabane" gets tip-offs from the police. The Cask is a proper boozer with a wide selection of Real Ale plus draft and bottled lagers and whisky. Great place to watch football or rugby as they have half a dozen TV screens.

voyage.name: The Cumberland Bar
voyage.hours: Mon-Thu 4:30-11PM, Fri Sat noon-midnight, Sun noon-11PM
voyage.content: Readers of Alexander McCall Smith's 44 Scotland Street will recognise this literary haunt. It's a traditional pub popular with New Town locals, students, the suits from local offices, pretty much everyone in fact. Gets very busy in summer thanks to its lovely beer garden - one of the few central pubs to have one. Plenty of drink options and decent food.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Gin Distillery
voyage.content: Micro-distillery producing gin in various styles. In summer 2024 they plan to move to larger premises on Market St near the station.

voyage.name: easyHotel.com Edinburgh
voyage.content: Tiny rooms, but right in the heart of the city facing the castle and Princes Street Gardens. Some rooms have no window.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Central Youth Hostel
voyage.content: Large hostel near the top of Leith Walk, about 10 minutes walk from Waverley Station. It serves meals and the cafe is open to the public. There is also a self-catering kitchen, and plasma screens abound. In addition to dormitories, some rooms (including singles) are available.

voyage.name: ibis Styles St Andrew Square
voyage.content: Good value Accor chain hotel 100 yards from the bus station.

voyage.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh City Centre (York Place)
voyage.content: Reliable chain hotel with spacious rooms for the price, and a/c. Some rooms have views over the New Town and Forth.

voyage.name: Cityroomz
voyage.content: Bright modern place at the west end of Princes St.

voyage.name: B+B Edinburgh
voyage.content: Traditional hotel with lovely views, but the lift is chronically out of action.

voyage.name: Tigerlily
voyage.content: Jazzy hotel near Charlotte Square, spacious rooms. No dogs.
Restaurant in a Georgian town house with four rooms. No dogs.

voyage.name: The Hoxton
voyage.content: The former Grosvenor re-opened in 2025, so it's sparkling fresh and eager to please.

voyage.name: Parliament House Hotel
voyage.content: Quiet backwater off busy streets at the foot of Calton Hill. Comfy and great value, tiny bathrooms.

voyage.name: Number 11
voyage.content: Slick welcoming hotel with great dining.

voyage.name: Waldorf Astoria Edinburgh
voyage.content: Grand hotel presiding over the west end of Princes St, facing the castle. It was built as the terminus station and hotel for the Caledonian Railway, vying with the rival North British terminus at the east end, now Waverley. The latter became the definitive city terminus, the west end station was demolished in 1970 and "The Caley" was able to expand. Citizens also discovered that it was rose pink, when 70 years of gri

voyage.name: InterContinental The George Hotel
voyage.content: 249-room hotel on busy George Street. The hotel was built as townhouses in the 1780s and knocked through into a hotel in 1881. Great scores for comfort, service and location.

voyage.name: Old Waverley Hotel
voyage.content: Very central location, but poky old rooms and no lift.

voyage.name: Balmoral Hotel
voyage.content: This baronial pile opened in 1902 as the terminus and hotel of the North British Railway, just pipping the rival Caledonian at the other end of Princes St. Its landmark clock tower is always three minutes fast to speed dawdlers towards their train. The NB Hotel was rebuilt to become the Balmoral in 1990. Great service and trad ambience, some visitors found it dated.

voyage.name: Nira Caledonia
voyage.content: Hotel (more like a B&B) at the edge of Stockbridge. Tiny rooms and beds, tall guests will suffer.

voyage.name: Kimpton Charlotte Square Hotel
voyage.content: On a charming garden squares, this 199-room was seven inter-connecting Georgian townhouses, built in 1791 to a design by Robert Adam, and converted to a hotel in 1881.

voyage.name: Cheval Edinburgh Grand
voyage.content: Plush studios and apartments between railway and bus stations.

voyage.name: The Glasshouse
voyage.content: Comfy central hotel, service spasmodic.

voyage.name: Royal Botanic Garden
voyage.hours: Daily Nov-Jan 10AM-4PM, Feb-Oct 10AM-5PM, last entry 15 min before closure
voyage.address: Inverleith Row for East Gate, Arboretum Place for West Gate
voyage.content: Impressive gardens with a large collection. Great place to wander around on a sunny day, or to sit and have a picnic. Highlights include the Rock Garden; the 165-m-long herbaceous border, backed by a huge, century-old beech hedge, and the Palm House, the tallest of its kind in Britain. The Palm House reopened in October 2026 after a big restoration, and you can only see it on pre-booked tours. (However all the other

voyage.name: Patriothall Gallery
voyage.content: Small art gallery and artists studios in the former co-op bakery. The gallery has regular exhibitions of modern art. The studios are open.on one weekend in mid-August and another in late November.

voyage.name: Fettes College
voyage.content: Boarding school in an impressive building in the style of a French Château by David Bryce built between 1863 and 1869. It can be seen from far away. Not open for tourists - the best view is looking through the fence from Carrington Road.

voyage.name: Museum of Scottish Fire Heritage
voyage.content: Volunteer-run museum within McDonald Road fire station. History of Scottish firefighting from the era of rival commercial fire companies, through early wooden fire engines to more recent appliances.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Academicals
voyage.content: "The Accies" were promoted in 2026 and now play rugby union in the Premiership, the amateur top tier in Scotland. Their home ground Raeburn Place (capacity 5000) staged the world's first rugby international on 27 March 1871. Scotland scored two tries and England scored one, so the result was 1-0 - a "try" in those days only gave you a chance to kick at goal.

voyage.name: The Grange
voyage.content: This is the usual home ground for the Scottish national team, the Saltires. They play 50-over and 20-over matches but not five-day Tests. Gen!us Grange play in the domestic leagues.

voyage.name: Glenogle Swim Centre
voyage.content: Council-run Victorian swimming pool with partial glass roof. Also has a gym and sauna.

voyage.name: King George V Park
voyage.content: Park with a couple of children's play areas and many quiet benches to sit on. A path through an old railway tunnel links the park with Cannonmills Tesco, making this an ideal lunch spot.

voyage.name: Inverleith Park
voyage.content: Large park with several sports pitches for rugby, football and cricket, and public tennis courts. The south of the park has a pond divided into a wildlife area popular with swans, and a boating pond which is often used for model boats. The banked area near the pond offers good views over the New Town of the Castle, and there is a small floral area in the Sundial Garden.

voyage.name: Rare Birds Book Shop
voyage.content: Specialising in books by women writers.

voyage.name: Sheila Fleet
voyage.content: Jewellery designer whose work reflects the lore and natural world of her native Orkney.

voyage.name: VoxBox Music
voyage.hours: Wed Sun noon-5PM, Sat 11AM-5PM, Sun noon-4PM
voyage.content: An independent record shop. They sell a range of collectible records, mainly used vinyl but also some new CDs and box sets.

voyage.name: IJ Mellis
voyage.content: Specialist cheesemonger with a range of farmhouse and artisan cheeses from all over Scotland, the UK and Europe. Their other branches are in Morningside, Victoria St, Glasgow and St Andrews.

voyage.name: Edina Lock & Key
voyage.content: Ironmonger and locksmith. If you like the brass door furniture you've seen on the traditional townhouses in the New Town, this is the place to pick up the knobs, knockers, numbers and letter-boxes you need to make your own front door look the same. A real treasure-trove of a shop.

voyage.name: The Bailie
voyage.content: Lovely old trad basement pub, known as much for its ale as its food. Standard pub-grub menu, but quality and prices are a notch higher.

voyage.name: Avery
voyage.content: Innovative Scots fare in a restaurant with one Michelin Star.

voyage.name: The Raeburn
voyage.content: Restaurant, pub, beer garden and small hotel in a house built in 1832.

voyage.name: Scran and Scallie
voyage.content: Upmarket gastro pub with modern Scots cuisine, slick service. They also run the Michelin-starred Kitchin in Leith.

voyage.name: Eòrna
voyage.content: Rave reviews for their Scottish fine dining. The name means "barley".

voyage.name: The Orchard
voyage.content: Friendly pub with bar meals, including gluten free.

voyage.name: Mimi's Bakehouse
voyage.content: Stockbridge branch of an Edinburgh chain of cafés, serving a fairly standard range of sandwiches, but interesting seasonal cakes and bakes.

voyage.name: Little Parlour
voyage.content: About 30 flavours of ice cream from Stewart Tower in Perthshire, and a selection of confectionery. The shop was opened as a Gentemen's Hairdressers in 1896 and continued as a barbers until 2024; the shop has only had small alterations for its present use.

voyage.name: The Stockbridge Tap
voyage.content: Trad bar with a good range of ales and whiskies, and a limited food selection.

voyage.name: Ardenlee Guest House
voyage.content: Pleasant Victorian terrace B&B half a mile from Princes Street.

voyage.name: Canon Court Aparthotel
voyage.content: Offers a wide range or 1- and 2-bedroom serviced apartments for short term lettings, in a building near the Water of Leith.

voyage.name: Village Hotel Club
voyage.content: Chain hotel in an ugly black box building, comfy enough. The main draw is the large gym and pool, non-residents can get day passes for this. It has a car park (£5 per day midweek), restaurant and bar, and frequent buses into town.

voyage.name: Brig O' Doon Guest House
voyage.content: Cosy friendly B&B by Goldenacres sports ground. Frequent buses to town centre. It's owned by Ardleigh House next door, which gets poor reviews and is overpriced.

voyage.name: Dr Neil's Garden
voyage.content: Secluded terraced garden on the shores of the loch, behind the church. The Neils were a GP couple who laid out the garden in the 1960s. The little tower, built 1825, is not to ward off body-snatchers but a storage space for the heavy curling stones.

voyage.name: Portobello Swim Centre
voyage.content: Traditional Victorian baths with pool, gym, sauna and Turkish Baths. Visitors often find the place cold and dirty.

voyage.name: Fort Kinnaird
voyage.content: A massive out-of-town retail complex (supposedly the biggest of its type in the UK), next to the A1 dual carriageway as it heads out of town to the south-east. Lots of mainstream chain shops.

voyage.name: Bonoful
voyage.content: Reliable place for Indian food.

voyage.name: Foresters Guild
voyage.hours: Mon-Thu noon-11PM, Fri noon-1AM, Sat 10AM-1AM, Sun 10AM-11PM
voyage.content: Good pub fare and cask ales, inside or in one of their beach huts.

voyage.name: Malvarosa
voyage.content: Good selection of tapas and slick service.

voyage.name: The Beach House
voyage.content: Right by the beach with sea views, good selection of food.

voyage.name: Mouse Hole Deli
voyage.content: Good value deli for takeaway food.

voyage.name: Cherry's Cafe
voyage.content: A small cafe serving Turkish food and breakfast.

voyage.name: Sheep Heid Inn
voyage.content: 18th-century pub, with implausible claims to date from 1360, and perhaps named for the village slaughter-ground. In 1745 Bonnie Prince Charlie's army camped outside for a month and he held a Council of War here, to good effect as he proceeded to beat Jonny Cope at the Battle of Prestonpans. The skittle alley dates from 1880. The Inn serves good food, with a popular Sunday roast.

voyage.name: The Regent
voyage.content: LGBT+ and straight-friendly bar with real ale.

voyage.name: Abercorn Guest House
voyage.content: Pleasant B&B close to the beach. Free parking, no pets.

voyage.name: Straven Guest House
voyage.content: Friendly small B&B close to the beach. No children under 12 or pets.

voyage.name: Seabreeze
voyage.content: Friendly spotless B&B east end of the beach.

voyage.name: Kings Manor Hotel
voyage.content: Friendly comfy mid-price hotel near Brunstane station.

voyage.name: The Brae
voyage.content: Small welcoming B&B on the A1.

voyage.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh East
voyage.content: Reliable chain offering, on A1 yet quiet.

voyage.name: Upright Gallery
voyage.content: Small gallery of local artists' work.

voyage.name: Royal Observatory
voyage.content: This opened in 1896 to replace the observatory on Calton Hill in New Town (which remained active to 2009 but is now an art exhibition space). The ROE is owned by the Science and Technology Facilities Council and houses the University of Edinburgh's Institute for Astronomy. Public evenings in winter are on Tuesday (booking essential) with talks and tours of the site.

voyage.name: Craigmillar Castle
voyage.content: Extensive ruin of a medieval castle, built from the 14th century and abandoned in the 18th. Here was hatched the plot to murder Lord Darnley, the inconvenient husband of Mary Queen of Scots. He was blown up at Kirk O'Field (now the site of the university Old College) and when that didn't do the job he was smothered.

voyage.name: Summerhall
voyage.content: Contemporary art exhibitions and event venue in a confident Edwardian building, home of Royal (Dick) School of Veterinary Studies from 1916. In 2011 the vets moved out to Easter Bush campus, birthplace of Dolly the Sheep. See below for the distillery, brewery and pub within Summerhall.

voyage.name: The Queen's Hall
voyage.content: Performance space for musical events across all genres. The neo-classical building was a chapel from 1824 and converted to a concert hall in 1979, with a capacity of 900.

voyage.name: Royal Commonwealth Pool
voyage.content: The pool was built for the Commonwealth Games in 1970, and was used again for the 1986 and 2014 games.

voyage.name: Dominion Cinema
voyage.content: Art deco cinema opened in 1938 with plush leather sofas for an upscale experience.

voyage.name: Midlothian Snowsports Centre
voyage.content: This has a main slope of 400 m, a loop alongside, 3 nursery slopes, a chairlift and 2 tows. Equipment hire is available or bring your own. Wear long trousers, long sleeves and gloves as the dendrex matting will skin you when you fall. Some disruption as a restaurant and other facilities are being built, and limited parking.

voyage.name: Scotmid Coop
voyage.content: Convenience supermarket in Tolcross.

voyage.name: Drinkmonger
voyage.content: They offer a very good selection of whiskies, wines, beers and other spirits.

voyage.name: Waitrose
voyage.content: A branch of the national supermarket chain. Free rooftop parking.

voyage.name: Great Grog
voyage.content: Independent store with a good selection of local and international beers, wines and spirits.

voyage.name: Cameron Toll
voyage.content: Large shopping centre with Aldi and Sainsburys supermarkets, other chain stores and filling station.

voyage.name: Susie's Vegetarian Kitchen
voyage.content: Vegetarian wraps, burritos and burgers.

voyage.name: The Wee Boulangerie
voyage.content: Delicious French bakery for breads, croissants, baguettes and so on. Mostly takeaway but they have a few tables to sit in.

voyage.name: Chaskaa
voyage.content: Modern Indian restaurant, consistently high quality.

voyage.name: Hendersons
voyage.content: Renowned vegetarian restaurant, run by the family of the original Hendersons in Hanover St which was open from 1962-2020. Michelin gives it an entry in their guide.

voyage.name: LeftField
voyage.content: This cosy seafood bistro gets great reviews.

voyage.name: Three Birds
voyage.content: Fine dining with a classic British menu, but almost entirely GF and much is vegan.

voyage.name: The Clay Oven
voyage.content: Takeaway offering trad Indian cuisine, fully halal.

voyage.name: Bakery Andante
voyage.content: Small bakery chain with three other city outlets.

voyage.name: Hermitage Bar
voyage.content: This pub has very good food at reasonable prices and a pleasant modern interior.

voyage.name: Voujon
voyage.content: Reliable North Indian / Bangladeshi restaurant.

voyage.name: Cask and Barrel
voyage.content: Trad pub with a central horseshoe bar, good selection of ale and whisky. No food. They have another pub on Broughton St in New Town.

voyage.name: Leslie's Bar
voyage.content: A trad pub with charming 1890s interior, dog-friendly, changing guest ales and a decent selection of whiskies.

voyage.name: Golf Tavern
voyage.content: Good food and an outside seating area facing Bruntsfield Links. You can hire golf clubs and balls here to play on the Links.

voyage.name: Canny Man's
voyage.content: Famously idiosyncratic pub with quirky decor, excellent range of ales, impressive choice of wine and whisky, and decent food.

voyage.name: Holyrood Distillery
voyage.content: Small distillery making whisky, vodka, gin and rum. Established in 2019, their first whisky went on sale in 2023.

voyage.name: Argyle Backpackers
voyage.content: Mixed reviews, good facilities, definitely not a party hostel.

voyage.name: University of Edinburgh Pollock Halls
voyage.content: University student accommodation is available to others from last week in June to first week in September. Their main site is Pollock Halls, where you might be in Baird House, Chancellor's Court, Scholar's Hotel or Scott Hotel. They also run KM Hotel half a mile north at the edge of Old Town.

voyage.name: Mortonhall Caravan & Camping Park
voyage.content: Clean spacious site open all year, with good facilities and buses to town.

voyage.name: The Bruntsfield
voyage.content: Traditional hotel a 15 min walk to Old Town. Pets welcome.

voyage.name: Southside Guest House
voyage.content: This changed owners in 2022 and quality has dipped, but it's still a decent mid-price option.

voyage.name: 94DR
voyage.content: This 6-bedroom villa is now only available to book on an exclusive basis by the week, and no longer a standard B&B.

voyage.name: Kingsway Guest House
voyage.content: Smart friendly guest house in a quiet spot.

voyage.name: Sonas Guest House
voyage.content: Pleasant B&B in an 1870s villa. Parking for cars, but no motorbikes accepted.

voyage.name: 23 Mayfield
voyage.content: Outstanding B&B with 7 rooms in a smartly decorated Victorian house. No children under 7.

voyage.name: Travelodge Cameron Toll
voyage.content: Usual Travelodge chain experience, good value for what you pay.

voyage.name: Prestonfield House
voyage.content: On the site of a former monastery hence "Priestfield", this was built in 1687 as a country mansion, and is now an upscale hotel with 23 rooms near the foot of Arthur's Seat. Rave reviews for comfort, service and cuisine, and it often hosts events. Wedding parties should mind where they pose, as Highland cattle graze in its grounds.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Printmakers
voyage.hours: Sun & Mon closed; Tue 10:00-17:30; Wed & Thu 10:00-21:00; Fri & Sat 10:17:30
voyage.content: Creative centre for printmaking & visual arts, Two free galleries & shop. Vegan Cafe.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Zoo
voyage.content: The pandas have returned to China but there's still plenty here. Penguins include gentoo, rockhopper and king, most famously Major General Sir Nils Olav III, Baron of the Bouvet Islands and mascot of the Norwegian King's Guard. Budongo Trail leads through the troupe of 15 chimpanzees. The only koalas in the UK are here, and there are some beautiful tropical birds. The zoo is on the slopes of Corstorphine Hill and som

voyage.name: Corstorphine Old Parish Church
voyage.content: The present building is a collegiate church of 1429, becoming a parish church in 1646, and re-modeled in 1828.

voyage.name: Lauriston Castle
voyage.content: This 1590s tower house was extended in the 1820s and housed a series of prosperous families. It passed into council ownership in 1926 and the interior has been preserved in its last occupants' plush Edwardian style. Visit by pre-booked guided tour. There is free entry to the gardens (daily 8AM-4:30PM), where the centrepiece is the Japanese garden. The castle is also used as an event space.

voyage.name: Murrayfield Stadium
voyage.content: The main stadium has a capacity of 67,000 and hosts all Scottish rugby internationals. The premier tournament is the Six Nations held each February-March: in odd-numbered years, Scotland hosts Wales, Ireland and Italy, and in even-numbered years the visitors are England and France. These games almost always sell out, and the city is mobbed when they're on; you've more chance of tickets and accommodation for other int

voyage.name: Murrayfield Ice Rink
voyage.hours: Mon 2-7PM, Wed Thu 2-9PM, Fri Sat 10AM-9PM, Sun 11:30AM-7PM
voyage.content: Popular ice rink with leisure skating sessions, and ice-discos on Friday and Saturday nights. It's the home rink of the Edinburgh Capitals ice hockey team, who play Sept-March in the Scottish National League, the UK second tier. (Their rivals Murrayfield Racers folded in 2022.) The curling club also play here on a separate rink.

voyage.name: Cineworld
voyage.content: Mainly mainstream cinema with some art-house & foreign cinema. IMAX screen.

voyage.name: Royal Highland Showground
voyage.content: An exhibition ground with several halls and large grounds. The premier event is the Royal Highland Show for 4 days in late June. Other events are held throughout the year, some of these are public, others are trade only.

voyage.name: Edinburgh International Climbing Arena
voyage.content: Huge indoor and outdoor climbing centre in a disused quarry, developed from 1995 but taken over and completed by Edinburgh City Council in 2007.

voyage.name: Heart of Midlothian
voyage.content: Hearts aka "the Jambos" and "the Gorgie Boys" play soccer in the Scottish Premiership, the top tier. Their home ground Tynecastle Park (capacity 20,000, all-seater) is a mile west of Haymarket station in the Gorgie area of the city; take any bus up Gorgie Road or a tram to Murrayfield.

voyage.name: Spartans
voyage.content: The Spartans play soccer in Scottish League Two, the fourth tier. Their ground Ainslie Park (Vanloq Community Stadium) holds 3612, of which 534 are seated. It's in Pilton, northwest of the city centre.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Filmhouse
voyage.price: £12 adult, £10.50 concession, wheelchair users/access tickets £5, carers free
voyage.content: A four-screen Edinburgh institution showing largely arthouse and some mainstream films. Additionally houses a 100-seat cafe-bar.

voyage.name: Corstorphine Retail Park
voyage.content: Small retail park with fast food, Lidl and a large Tesco, overshadowed nowadays by the Gyle Centre.

voyage.name: Gyle Shopping Centre
voyage.content: Indoor shopping centre with Marks and Spencer, Morrisons and some 50 other shops.

voyage.name: First Coast
voyage.content: Long-standing bistro serving quality Scots cuisine.

voyage.name: Masti
voyage.content: Classic North Indian Balti menu.

voyage.name: Miller & Carter Cramond Brig
voyage.content: Popular chain steakhouse getting great reviews. The old Cramond Brig is now a footbridge over River Almond, follow the east bank for the village and island, and the west bank to hike to South Queensferry. Modern traffic thunders past on A90.

voyage.name: Holy Cow Lounge
voyage.content: Vegan cafe in Edinburgh Printmakers building.

voyage.name: The Murrayfield
voyage.content: Friendly pub close to Murrayfield Stadium with screens for TV sport. Decent all-day pub grub.

voyage.name: Cramond Inn
voyage.content: Traditional village pub run by Samuel Smiths. Beer garden outside but food service is indoors-only. No dogs.

voyage.name: Bainfield
voyage.content: This is single-room student accommodation for Napier University but available to others during the summer break.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn Edinburgh
voyage.content: Simple value hotel with restaurant. Those strange noises are from the zoo animals next door.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn Express Edinburgh City West
voyage.content: Acceptable rooms, variable welcome and service.

voyage.name: White Lady
voyage.content: Small hotel on the Glasgow Rd run by JD Wetherspoon. Frequent buses to city centre.

voyage.name: Leonardo
voyage.content: Value-for-money hotel on Corstorphine Hill, calls itself "Murrayfield" which is two miles southeast.

voyage.name: Bridge Inn
voyage.content: On the canal, and most customers are just here for the excellent dining, but the snug rooms are well worth a stay. Closed for maintenance until March 2024.

voyage.name: Hampton by Hilton Edinburgh Airport
voyage.content: The closest to the terminal, a 300 yard walk, this is comfy and efficient.

voyage.name: Doubletree by Hilton Edinburgh Airport
voyage.content: Comfy hotel a 10-minute walk from the terminal.

voyage.name: Moxy Edinburgh Airport
voyage.content: Modern hotel with small, comfortable rooms and friendly staff. It's a 10-minute walk from the terminal - head for the trams, then follow the signs pointing to the Doubletree Hotel.

voyage.name: Holiday Inn Express
voyage.content: A bit frayed but overall good value. It's by the Showground, a 20-minute walk from the terminal so take their shuttle bus.

voyage.name: Travelodge Edinburgh Airport
voyage.address: Ratho Park, off Station Rd, Ratho Station EH28 8PP
voyage.content: Value hotel two miles west of airport with shuttle bus.

voyage.name: Premier Inn Edinburgh Airport
voyage.content: Reliable chain hotel three miles west of airport with shuttle bus.

voyage.name: The Roseate
voyage.content: Mixed reviews - the main building is okay, but some rooms are in a basement across the road and not worth the money.

voyage.name: Novotel Edinburgh Park
voyage.content: Unlovely area of light industry and retail, but the hotel is next to M8 / city bypass interchange and Edinburgh Park Station. It has a pool, gym, steam room and restaurant.

voyage.name: Norton House Hotel
voyage.content: Villa built in 1840 as country retreat, and now a hotel and spa in woodland close to the airport. Great welcome and service, smart modern interior. It's 10 mins walk to main bus routes on the road to Glasgow, but you really ought to be arriving by limo or helicopter. It hosts a lot of functions for people who wished they were.

voyage.name: Dalmahoy
voyage.content: Grand pile built in 1725 and much extended since, it's now an upscale hotel and golf resort.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Castle
voyage.price: Adult £19.50, child (7-15) £11.40, conc £15.50, Historic Scotland / English Heritage / Cadw free
voyage.content: Iconic fortress perched magnificently on a volcanic rock above the city. The castle has been continuously used for 1100 years and is kept in excellent condition; it's still the ceremonial headquarters of the army in Scotland. Highlights include the Great Hall, the Honours of Scotland (the Scottish Crown Jewels), the War Museum and the 12th century St Margaret's Chapel. The One O'Clock Gun is fired each day from Mills

voyage.name: Camera Obscura
voyage.content: Over 150 years old, the Camera Obscura projects light from the top of the tower onto a large dish in a dark room below, displaying a panorama of the city. The effect still works on overcast days or at night but is best in sunlight, when you can use a sheet of paper to "pick up" people seen in the streets and have them scurry in your hand. The tower also houses a gallery of optical illusions that wouldn't be out of pl

voyage.name: Gladstone's Land
voyage.price: Adult £10, conc £8.50, child £6, NTS / NT free
voyage.content: Thomas Gladstone was a wealthy merchant, and in 1617 he had this house refashioned to accommodate his family and to partly rent out. A "Land" means a tall narrow townhouse from the period when Old Town was cramped and the only space for development was upwards. Typically along the Royal Mile the ground floor was shops and trade, genteel folk lived on the first and second floors, and lower-income residents had to lump

voyage.name: Writers' Museum
voyage.content: This museum, in a tall house built in 1622, celebrates three Scottish literary giants: Robert Burns, Sir Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson. From 1719 the close was the residence of the widow of the 1st Earl of Stair, who ordered the Glencoe massacre.

voyage.name: St Giles
voyage.content: It's often called a Cathedral, but the Church of Scotland brooks no such episcopal entity, and Charles I dubbing it "cathedral" in 1633 was one reason his head was chopped off. Safer to call it "High Kirk", though they're nowadays lenient with first time offenders. The present building is from 14th century with much Victorian Gothic, notably its crowned spire. Highlight is the Chapel of the Order of the Thistle, Scot

voyage.name: Mary King's Close
voyage.content: Mary King (1590-1644) was a clothes merchant and city burgess. She died the year before plague struck and carried off the rest of her family. In 1753 Royal Exchange, now City Chambers, was built over several closes by demolishing their upper storeys, while the lower storeys were used for storage then later blocked off. This means a warren of medieval alleys and low dwellings has been preserved, re-opened in 2003 and

voyage.name: Museum of Childhood
voyage.content: Concepts and imagery of childhood are ever-changing. See if you can find your (or your grandparents') old toys in the collection, and your place in history.

voyage.name: The Peoples' Story Museum
voyage.content: This is housed in Canongate Tolbooth, the medieval centre for governance and justice (preferably gruesome) as Canongate was a separate jurisdiction until 1856. The museum covers the story of working class life, and of organised labour, from the late 18th century to the present.

voyage.name: Canongate Kirk
voyage.hours: Open Sun afternoon, otherwise erratic; Services Sun 10:30
voyage.content: In 1687 James VII (II of England) chucked the Protestants out of Holyrood to convert it to a royal Roman Catholic chapel, the sort of behaviour that got him ousted from the monarchy the following year. The congregation moved to Infirmary St then to this building on its completion in 1691. From 1952 Queen Elizabeth II regularly attended when at Holyrood, and in 2011 her granddaughter Zara Phillips married former Engla

voyage.name: Museum of Edinburgh
voyage.content: Museum of city history in a mustard-hued mansion built in 1570.

voyage.name: Dunbar's Close Garden
voyage.content: This close was re-modelled in the 1970s to recreate a 17th-century physic and knot garden, a hidden quiet place in the busy city.

voyage.name: Scottish Parliament
voyage.hours: Mon Fri Sat and public holidays 10AM-5PM, Tue-Thu 9AM-6:30PM
voyage.content: A unique building, designed by Spanish Catalan architect Enric Miralles, completed in 2004. It's either a daring showpiece of postmodern architecture or a national embarrassment or a bit of both, time will tell. Parliament meets Tu-Th and you can watch debates from the Public Gallery, ask for tickets at reception. First Minister's Question Time is normally Th noon-12:45PM, and you need to reserve this up to 7 days in

voyage.name: Dynamic Earth
voyage.content: Interactive natural history museum exhibiting the forces and features of our planet: volcanoes, polar ice, rainforests and so on. Opened in 1999, it's a tent-like structure on the former site of a gasworks and brewery.

voyage.name: Holyrood Palace
voyage.hours: Nov-Mar Thu-Mon 9:30AM - 4:30PM, Apr-Oct Thu-Mon (& daily Jul-Sep) 9:30AM - 6PM
voyage.content: The Palace is a royal residence, closed when the king is here for a week in July and for similar state occasions. It's been repeatedly smashed up and rebuilt, and the present building is mostly from the 1670s. Highlights are the grand stair, state apartments, throne room, Mary Queen of Scots Chambers (where bloodstains from the murder of Rizzio are still visible), King's Gallery a sample of the royal art collection,

voyage.name: George IV Bridge
voyage.content: This high-level road courses south from the top of High Street and spans the hollow of Grassmarket. Completed in 1836, it's lined with Victorian and modern buildings such as the two libraries. Victoria Street descends into the hollow, while Victoria Terrace is a walkway above it that loops back onto Royal Mile.

voyage.name: National Library of Scotland
voyage.content: A venerable reference library, which you need membership to access, but it has public exhibitions about literature. "Treasures" is its permanent exhibition. But don't stumble in here mistaking it for Central Library across the street.

voyage.name: Central Library
voyage.content: See Edinburgh#Connect for how to access. The internet stations are in the Learning Centre, and the building houses Central Lending Library, Central Reference Library, Central Children's Library, Edinburgh and Scottish Collections, Art & Design Library and Music Library. It has a wealth of material for research such as old newspapers and maps, but births, marriages and deaths are filed at East Register House by the bu

voyage.name: Greyfriars Kirk
voyage.content: This church was built in 1620 on the grounds of an abandoned Franciscan Friary, but seriously damaged by later calamities or Acts of God so the present structure is mostly Victorian. It remains active, as other Presbyterian churches have closed and their congregations moved here. The main visitor interest is the ancient graveyard: notable denizens include the architects William and John Adam, the notorious hell-rake

voyage.name: National Museum of Scotland
voyage.content: Superb museum of Scotland's heritage. You enter into the lofty Victorian Grand Gallery, where the millennium clock chimes on the hour. Exhibition halls cover Scottish and world history and culture, science, technology, art and design, and natural history. Dolly the sheep, the 12th-century Lewis chess pieces, and dinosaurs are some of the highlights. NMS also run the War Museum in the castle, the Museum of Flight near

voyage.name: Anatomical Museum
voyage.hours: Last Sat of Sept-Nov and Jan-May
voyage.address: Doorway 3, Medical School, Teviot Place EH8 9AG
voyage.content: Large collection of anatomical specimens and life and death masks. Best known is the skeleton of William Burke, hanged in 1829 after he and William Hare killed at least 16 people to sell the bodies for dissection. Limited opening as the area is in continual use for teaching, booking essential.

voyage.name: St Cecilia's Hall
voyage.content: Scotland's oldest purpose-built concert hall, opened in 1763 and still in regular use. It hosts the University of Edinburgh collection of historic musical instruments, crafted 16th to 20th century, many of which (such as the Trompette Demilune) are no longer played.

voyage.name: Talbot Rice Gallery
voyage.content: David Talbot Rice (1903-72) was in the louche crowd at Oxford that inspired Brideshead Revisited and became a distinguished scholar of East Mediterranean and Russian art, with extensive contacts in those parts - how come this fellow was never implicated in a spy ring? His spell as University Vice Principal is commemorated in this gallery with changing exhibitions of contemporary art. It's housed within Old College of

voyage.name: Dovecot Studios
voyage.content: Tapestry studio and gallery housed in the former public baths. There is a cafe, shop, and viewing gallery where you can look down on weavers at work.

voyage.name: Surgeons' Hall Museums
voyage.content: The permanent exhibitions are the Pathology Museum, the History of Surgery and the Dental Museum. Not suitable for children under 10 as the exhibits include human remains.

voyage.name: Edinburgh Central Mosque
voyage.content: Stately mosque and minaret completed in 1998 in a modern variant of Turkish style. You can generally look in between prayer times.

voyage.name: City Art Centre
voyage.content: Four-floor gallery run by the city council. They rotate artwork from their extensive Scottish collection and have changing exhibitions.

voyage.name: Fruitmarket
voyage.content: Gallery of contemporary art, refurbished in 2018. From 1936 to the 1970s this was where soft fruit and veg were traded, handy for the trains and delivery vans.

voyage.name: Stills
voyage.content: Photography gallery with three exhibitions a year. They also support photographers through courses and hire of equipment, darkroom and digital lab.

voyage.name: Museum on the Mound
voyage.content: Museum about money and coins, in the basement of the Palladian pile of the former Bank of Scotland headquarters. Scotland developed a banking sector in the 18th century to support long-distance trade, and still prints its own banknotes.

voyage.name: The Edinburgh Dungeon
voyage.content: "Haunted House" experience, where you take a 70 min tour through 11 shows and 2 rides loosely based on Scotland's horrible history: William Wallace, Mary King's Ghost, cannibal Sawney Bean, Burke and Hare and more.

voyage.name: Escape The Past
voyage.content: Immersive escape rooms and outdoor puzzle trails based on Edinburgh's history. Experiences include historically accurate props, live actors and special effects. Housed in the basement of a 19th Century Methodist Church. Highlights include "The Anatomist" a 60 minute escape room based on Edinburgh's grave-robbing-era medical history.

voyage.name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
voyage.content: Tour of the history and craft of whisky distilling, with expert guides - the basic or "silver" tour works well for beginners. They have a huge selection; the core of it is the 3384 bottles collected by Brazilian whisky enthusiast Claive Vidiz.

voyage.name: The Lost Close
voyage.content: Underground experiences and tours led by expert Storytellers. Whisky, gin and beer tastings available - starting from £15.

voyage.name: Monkey Barrel Comedy
voyage.content: Intimate comedy venue with several acts each night. Drink and some food available.

voyage.name: Festival Theatre
voyage.content: Large performance venue, home of the Scottish Ballet and Scottish Opera. It also hosts contemporary dance, ballet, musicals and panto.

voyage.name: Reid Concert Hall
voyage.content: General Reid (1721-1807) endowed the School of Music at the University of Edinburgh. They put on occasional free lunchtime concerts here, especially on 13 Feb, Reid's birthday. You may also be able to look in on their collection of antique instruments.

voyage.name: Usher Hall
